name: Gold Standard / Official Price Era
summary: Gold convertibility and a government-fixed official price. $20.67/oz under the classical gold standard until the 1934 Gold Reserve Act revalued gold to $35/oz.
characteristics: Fixed official gold price set by statute

name: Bretton Woods
summary: Dollar-anchored system with gold convertible at $35/oz for foreign central banks. US held most monetary gold; the dollar became the global reserve currency.
characteristics: London Gold Pool (1961-1968) defended the price
Triffin dilemma: reserve demand vs. gold backing

name: Post-Bretton-Woods Fiat Transition
summary: Nixon Shock ended convertibility in 1971. Gold floated freely for the first time in the modern era as the world moved to fiat money amid oil shocks and stagflation.

name: Great Inflation Gold Bull Market
summary: Runaway inflation, dollar weakness, and geopolitical shocks drove gold from ~$125 to a January 1980 peak near $850.
characteristics: Iran hostage crisis; Soviet invasion of Afghanistan

name: Strong-Dollar Disinflation Era
summary: The Volcker shock and high real rates crushed inflation. A strong dollar, equity bull market, and central bank gold sales produced a two-decade gold bear market.
characteristics: Central bank gold sales (Washington Agreement 1999 capped them)

name: Post-Dotcom & GFC Monetary Expansion
summary: Serial monetary easing after the dot-com bust, the 2008 Global Financial Crisis, and the eurozone crisis. Zero rates, quantitative easing, and ETF access drove gold to a 2011 peak near $1900, then a real-rate-driven bear into 2015.
characteristics: Zero/low policy rates and multiple QE rounds

name: 2020s Inflation & Geopolitical Reserve Diversification
summary: COVID stimulus, the highest inflation in 40 years, the 2022 freezing of Russian reserves, and record central bank buying drove gold to successive records and shifted reserve demand toward gold.
characteristics: 2022 reserve freeze reframed gold as sanction-proof reserve
